tagline: The last of the prophets argues with a tired, disillusioned people and promises that the Lord will send his messenger and come to his temple.
overview:
Malachi is the final book of the Old Testament in Christian Bibles and the last of the twelve shorter prophets. It speaks to Jews in Judah a few generations after the return from exile. The temple has been rebuilt and the sacrifices restored, but the great future the earlier prophets promised has not arrived. The people are still poor, still ruled by Persia, and increasingly cynical. Priests offer blind and lame animals, men divorce the wives of their youth, tithes go unpaid, and ordinary believers ask whether serving God is worth it at all.

The book is built as a series of arguments. God makes a statement, the people push back with a question (How have you loved us? How have we despised your name?), and God answers with evidence. Through these exchanges Malachi exposes a faith that has gone through the motions while its heart went cold, and he calls priests and people back to covenant loyalty. Then he looks forward: God will send his messenger to prepare the way, the Lord will suddenly come to his temple to refine his people like silver, and before the great day of the LORD Elijah the prophet will come to turn the hearts of fathers and children.

That promise matters enormously for the Bible as a whole. The Old Testament in its Christian order closes on the expectation of a coming messenger and an Elijah, and the New Testament opens with John the Baptist, dressed like Elijah, preparing the way for Jesus. Malachi is the hinge between the two.
author: The book's heading attributes it to Malachi (1:1), and nothing else is known of him. The name means my messenger, the same Hebrew form used in 3:1 (My messenger), which has led some to ask whether it is a title rather than a personal name. The ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, rendered 1:1 as by the hand of his messenger, and some early Jewish tradition identified the author with Ezra. The heading also resembles those at Zechariah 9:1 and 12:1, and many critical scholars suggest the book was originally an anonymous oracle given a name drawn from 3:1. Many other scholars, conservative and critical alike, take Malachi as a real prophet's name, noting that every other prophetic book is attributed to a named person and that similar names are attested. Either way, the book presents itself as the word of the LORD through a messenger, and its authority has never rested on knowing more about him.
date: The book gives no date, but its details point clearly to the Persian period after the exile. The temple is standing and sacrifices are offered (1:7-10), so it comes after 515 BC. Judah is under a governor, the Persian-era title used in 1:8. The abuses Malachi attacks, corrupt priests, marriages to women who worship other gods, and neglected tithes, are the same ones Ezra and Nehemiah confronted (Ezra 9-10; Nehemiah 13). Most scholars therefore date Malachi to the middle of the fifth century BC, around 470 to 430 BC. Some place it shortly before Ezra's arrival in 458 BC or Nehemiah's first term as governor beginning in 445 BC, preparing the ground for their reforms; others place it during the interval around Nehemiah's second visit, when the same problems had returned.
setting:
Judah was a small province, called Yehud, within the vast Persian Empire, ruled from Susa and Persepolis under kings such as Artaxerxes I (who reigned from 465 to 424 BC). Jerusalem was a modest town, and for much of this period its walls lay in ruins until Nehemiah rebuilt them. The returned exiles had been promised glory by Haggai and Zechariah, who urged the temple's rebuilding around 520 to 515 BC, but decades later there was no Davidic king, no wealth of the nations flowing in, and no visible sign that God was keeping his word.

That long disappointment bred a quiet cynicism. Priests treated the altar as a chore, offering sick animals they would never dare present to the governor. Men married women from surrounding peoples and discarded their first wives. Farmers held back the tithe that supported the Levites. And the devout watched the arrogant prosper and wondered aloud what they had gained by fearing the LORD. Meanwhile Edom, Judah's old rival to the southeast, had been devastated, its land slowly taken over by Arab peoples, and Malachi points to that ruin as evidence that God still distinguishes between nations.
purpose: Malachi was written to call a discouraged and compromised community back to wholehearted covenant faithfulness. It confronts the priests first, because they had corrupted worship and instruction, and then the people, for unfaithfulness in marriage, in giving, and in speech about God. Its deeper purpose is to answer the question behind all the complaints: does God still love us, and does faithfulness matter? Malachi answers yes on both counts, grounds that answer in God's unchanging character (3:6), and gives the faithful a future to wait for: a coming messenger, a coming Lord, a day that will burn like a furnace for the arrogant and rise like the sun for those who fear his name.
story: Malachi comes at the end of the Old Testament's story of return. After the Babylonian exile, Cyrus of Persia allowed the Jews to go home in 539/538 BC; the temple was rebuilt under Zerubbabel with the urging of Haggai and Zechariah; and Ezra and Nehemiah later reformed the community and rebuilt Jerusalem's walls. Malachi speaks into that same world, a generation or two after the temple's completion, when the energy of return has faded. In Christian Bibles, which follow the order of the Greek Old Testament, it is the last book before the Gospels, so its closing promise of Elijah leads straight into the New Testament. In the Hebrew Bible, Malachi closes the section of the Prophets, and the Writings follow, ending with Chronicles. Around four centuries pass between Malachi and the birth of Jesus, years of Persian, Greek, and then Roman rule.
christ:
The Gospels open where Malachi ends. Malachi 3:1 promises a messenger who will prepare the way before the LORD, and Mark begins his Gospel by quoting it together with Isaiah 40:3 (Mark 1:2-3). Jesus himself identifies John the Baptist as the messenger of Malachi 3:1 (Matthew 11:10) and says that John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:10-13). The angel's announcement of John's birth uses Malachi 4:6, saying John will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children (Luke 1:17). John himself, asked whether he was Elijah, said he was not (John 1:21), which most interpreters take to mean he was not Elijah returned in person, while he did come in the spirit and power of Elijah.

If John is the messenger who prepares the way, then the one who comes after him is the Lord who comes to his temple (3:1). The New Testament makes that identification of Jesus with the LORD of Israel quietly but unmistakably. Malachi's refining fire, his promise of pure offerings among the nations (1:11), and his sun of righteousness rising with healing (4:2) have all been read by Christians in light of Christ's coming, though these readings are more thematic than direct quotations.
reading: Read Malachi as a set of disputations: listen for the pattern of God's claim, the people's objection, and God's reply, and notice how the objections expose the people's hearts. The book is prophecy in prose with poetic touches, not a law code, so its sharp statements (Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated; I hate divorce) should be read within the argument each is making rather than lifted out as freestanding rules. Be aware that Hebrew Bibles have only three chapters; English 4:1-6 is Hebrew 3:19-24. Two common misreadings are worth avoiding. The tithing passage (3:6-12) is sometimes turned into a promise of personal wealth, but it addresses a covenant community's support of temple worship and its trust in God's provision. And the book's hard words against the priests and people are not the whole message; they sit inside God's opening declaration, I have loved you.

structure.title: God's love for Jacob
structure.summary: The first disputation answers the question how God has loved Israel by pointing to his choice of Jacob over Esau and the ruin of Edom.

structure.title: The priests who despise God's name
structure.summary: God indicts the priests for offering defective animals and for corrupting their calling to teach, contrasting them with the covenant faithfulness of Levi.

structure.title: Faithlessness in marriage
structure.summary: The people break faith with God and with one another by marrying worshipers of foreign gods and divorcing the wives of their youth.

structure.title: The coming messenger and the Lord's refining
structure.summary: To those who ask where the God of justice is, the LORD promises a messenger to prepare his way and his own sudden coming to refine and judge.

structure.title: Return and bring the tithe
structure.summary: God calls the people to return to him and to stop robbing him in tithes and offerings, promising blessing if they trust him.

structure.title: The day that is coming
structure.summary: To those who say serving God is futile, God promises a scroll of remembrance, a day of burning for the arrogant and healing for the faithful, and Elijah before the great day of the LORD.

themes.title: God's steadfast love
themes.body: The book begins with God's declaration, I have loved you, and every rebuke that follows is spoken from within that love. The choice of Jacob, the covenant with Levi, the covenant of marriage, and the unchanging character of the LORD (3:6) all rest on a love that precedes Israel's response and outlasts its failures.

themes.title: Worship that honors God
themes.body: Malachi insists that how people worship reveals what they think of God. Blind and lame sacrifices, grudging tithes, and bored priests say that God is not worth the best. The book contrasts that contempt with a coming day when God's name will be great among the nations and pure offerings will be brought in every place.

themes.title: Covenant faithfulness
themes.body: Covenant is the book's backbone: the covenant with Levi (2:4-8), the covenant of the fathers (2:10), the covenant of marriage (2:14), and the messenger of the covenant (3:1). Unfaithfulness to God and unfaithfulness to one another are treated as the same sin seen from two sides.

themes.title: The coming day of the LORD
themes.body: Against the complaint that God does not act, Malachi promises that he will: a messenger will prepare the way, the Lord will come to his temple, and a day is coming that will distinguish the righteous from the wicked. That day brings refining fire and burning for the arrogant, and healing and joy for those who fear God's name.

themes.title: Honest questions and cynical ones
themes.body: The people's questions run through the book, and Malachi distinguishes between them. Some are defensive evasions (How have we despised your name?). Some are the cynicism of people who have decided God does not care. And some come from the faithful who fear the LORD and talk together in their perplexity, and God listens and writes their names in a book of remembrance (3:16).

keyChapters.why: God's declaration of love and his rebuke of worthless worship set the terms of the whole book, and 1:11 promises that God's name will be great among the nations.
The chapter joins the corruption of the priesthood with unfaithfulness in marriage and gives one of the Old Testament's strongest statements of marriage as a covenant witnessed by God.
The promise of the messenger who prepares the way and the Lord who comes to his temple is quoted by the Gospels of John the Baptist and Jesus.
The Old Testament's final words point back to the law of Moses and forward to Elijah, and the New Testament opens by answering them.
